concepts.name: Election and Tenure of the Speaker
key_dimensions: Constitutional provisions: Article 178 — election by members of the Legislative Assembly from amongst themselves
Tenure trap: Speaker holds office during the pleasure of the House, NOT during the pleasure of the Governor
Vacation of office: When the Speaker ceases to be a member of the Assembly vs. resignation procedure (resignation addressed to Deputy Speaker)
Comparison with Lok Sabha Speaker's tenure and the subtle differences in removal procedure

concepts.name: Removal of the Speaker: Procedure and Conditions
key_dimensions: Article 179(c): Removal by a resolution passed by a majority of all then members of the Assembly — effective majority, not simple majority
Critical trap: 14-day advance notice is mandatory before moving such a resolution
Speaker's unique right to vote during the removal resolution proceedings — can vote in the first instance unlike normal presiding
Comparison with removal of the Governor (pleasure of President) to highlight the democratic accountability of the Speaker

concepts.name: Speaker's Role During Dissolution of the Assembly
key_dimensions: Article 179: Speaker does NOT vacate office merely because the Assembly is dissolved — continues until the new Assembly meets
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between dissolution (Speaker continues) vs. resignation/ceasing to be a member (vacates immediately)
Continuity principle: Ensures institutional continuity during the interregnum period
Contrast with Ministers who vacate on dissolution — highlights the Speaker's non-partisan constitutional role

concepts.name: Powers and Functions of the Speaker: Conduct of Business
key_dimensions: Adjournment of the House, sine die adjournment, and prorogation — Speaker adjourns; Governor prorogues
Casting vote: Speaker does NOT vote in the first instance but exercises casting vote in case of a tie
Certification of Money Bills under Article 199 — Speaker's certificate is final and cannot be questioned in any court
Power to disallow questions, expunge remarks from proceedings, and maintain order

concepts.name: Speaker and the Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)
key_dimensions: Speaker is the sole adjudicating authority for disqualification under the Tenth Schedule for the Legislative Assembly
Judicial review of Speaker's decision: Kihoto Hollohan case (1992) — Speaker's order IS subject to judicial review but only AFTER a final order, not at interim stage
Constitutional controversy: Speaker acting as judge in own cause when ruling party members face defection — conflict of interest debate
Recent controversies: Manipulation of disqualification proceedings (e.g., Manipur, Goa cases) and the Supreme Court's direction for time-bound decisions

concepts.name: Kihoto Hollohan Case (1992) and Its Implications for Speaker's Powers
key_dimensions: Upheld the Tenth Schedule as constitutionally valid but struck down paragraph 7 (which barred judicial review) as unconstitutional
Established that the Speaker acts as a 'tribunal' under the Tenth Schedule — decision has the force of law
Limitation imposed: Courts can intervene only after a final order by the Speaker, not during proceedings
Recent judicial pushback: Supreme Court's evolving position on time limits for Speaker to decide disqualification petitions (Subhash Desai case)

concepts.name: Speaker's Role in Certifying Money Bills
key_dimensions: Article 199 defines Money Bill for state legislatures — Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill
Finality clause: Speaker's decision is final — no court can question the certificate (contrast with judicial review in other matters)
UPSC trap: In a bicameral state legislature, the Legislative Council has no power to reject/amend a Money Bill; Speaker's certification triggers this
Controversy: Misuse of Money Bill certification to bypass the Upper House — parallels with Aadhaar Act controversy at the Centre

concepts.name: Speaker's Powers Regarding Committee System
key_dimensions: Speaker nominates members and chairpersons of various legislative committees (e.g., Business Advisory Committee, Public Accounts Committee)
Speaker is the ex-officio head of the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee
Power to refer Bills to Select/Joint Committees — Speaker decides the composition and terms of reference
Significance: Committee system is the Speaker's primary tool for detailed legislative scrutiny — often neglected in Indian state legislatures

concepts.name: Speaker's Powers to Maintain Order and Discipline
key_dimensions: Power to suspend members for disorderly conduct — distinction between suspension by Speaker vs. suspension by the House itself
Power to 'name' a member — a formal disciplinary action preceding suspension
Expunging of proceedings: Speaker can order deletion of objectionable remarks from the official record
Contempt of the House: Speaker's role in referring matters to the Privileges Committee vs. direct action

concepts.name: Privileges of the Speaker and Legislative Assembly Members
key_dimensions: Article 194: Collective and individual privileges of the state legislature — freedom of speech, immunity from court proceedings
Speaker's role as custodian and enforcer of privileges — decides whether a breach of privilege has occurred
Article 212: Courts cannot inquire into proceedings of the legislature — Speaker's rulings enjoy this immunity
UPSC trap: Privilege immunity is NOT absolute — courts can intervene if there is an allegation of unconstitutional action (Raja Ram Pal case)

concepts.name: Deputy Speaker: Role, Election, and Relationship with Speaker
key_dimensions: Article 178: Deputy Speaker is also elected by the Assembly — same procedure as Speaker
Convention (not constitutional requirement): Deputy Speaker is often elected from the opposition party in some states
UPSC trap: When both Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent, a member of the House (from the panel of chairpersons) presides — NOT the Governor
Deputy Speaker presides when the Speaker is absent OR when a resolution for the Speaker's removal is being considered — Speaker steps down

concepts.name: Speaker's Position During a No-Confidence Motion Against the Government
key_dimensions: Speaker's duty to allow and schedule the no-confidence motion — Speaker cannot indefinitely defer it (constitutional convention)
Controversy: Instances of Speakers deferring no-confidence motions to protect ruling governments (e.g., Arunachal Pradesh 2016)
Supreme Court in Nabam Rebia case (2016): If a notice of removal against the Speaker is pending, the Speaker cannot adjudicate disqualification petitions — critical limitation
Distinction: No-confidence motion against government vs. removal resolution against Speaker — different procedures and majorities

concepts.name: Nabam Rebia Case (2016) and Its Constitutional Significance
key_dimensions: SC held that when a notice of motion for the Speaker's removal is pending, the Speaker loses authority to decide disqualification petitions
Constitutional logic: Speaker cannot act as judge when their own removal is being sought — conflict of interest
Broader implication: Curtails Speaker's power under Tenth Schedule when the Speaker's own position is challenged
Referred to a larger Constitution Bench for reconsideration — the law is not yet fully settled; UPSC may test this evolving position

concepts.name: Impartiality of the Speaker: Constitutional Expectation vs. Political Reality
key_dimensions: Constitutional expectation: Speaker should be impartial and rise above party politics after election
Indian practice vs. UK convention: In UK, Speaker severs all party ties; in India, the Speaker typically remains a party member
Specific controversies: Speakers making partisan rulings on disqualification, deferring no-confidence motions, and certifying ordinary bills as Money Bills
Reform suggestions: N.C. Saxena Committee and various Law Commission recommendations for making the Speaker's office truly independent

concepts.name: Speaker's Role in Bicameral State Legislatures
key_dimensions: Only 6 states have bicameral legislatures (with Legislative Council) — UPSC trap on which states these are (UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, AP, Telangana)
Speaker presides ONLY over the Legislative Assembly; the Legislative Council is presided over by the Chairman
Joint sitting of both Houses: Unlike Parliament (Article 108), there is NO constitutional provision for a joint sitting of State Legislative Assembly and Council
Money Bill and deadlock resolution: No joint sitting means a deadlock between the two Houses cannot be resolved by joint sitting — Council's delaying power is the only check

concepts.name: Speaker's Secretariat and Administrative Powers
key_dimensions: The Speaker controls the Secretariat of the Legislative Assembly — independent of the state government's control
Recruitment and service conditions of Assembly Secretariat staff: Governed by rules made by the Speaker (not the State PSC)
Financial independence: The Assembly Secretariat's budget is typically a 'charged expenditure' on the Consolidated Fund of the State, not subject to vote
Significance for separation of powers: Administrative independence of the Speaker's office reinforces the legislature's independence from the executive

concepts.name: Distinction Between Speaker of Legislative Assembly and Chairman of Legislative Council
key_dimensions: Speaker is elected by members of the Assembly; Chairman of the Legislative Council is also elected by members of the Council
UPSC trap: The Vice-Chairman of the Council (not Chairman) presides when a resolution for Chairman's removal is being considered — parallel to Speaker/Deputy Speaker
Removal procedure is identical — majority of all then members of the respective House with 14-day notice
Functional difference: Chairman of Council does NOT certify Money Bills; that power rests exclusively with the Speaker of the Assembly

concepts.name: Constitutional Provisions: Articles 178–212 and Their Scope for State Legislature
key_dimensions: Article 178: Election of Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
Article 179: Vacation, resignation, and removal — the 'continues till new House meets' provision for Speaker post-dissolution
Article 180: Power of Deputy Speaker or other person to perform Speaker's duties during vacancy/absence
Articles 194 and 212: Privileges and immunity of proceedings — UPSC frequently tests whether courts can review legislative proceedings (answer: generally no, with exceptions)

concepts.name: Speaker's Role in Recognizing the Leader of Opposition and Party Whips
key_dimensions: Speaker formally recognizes the Leader of the Opposition — there is no statutory definition; it is based on the Speaker's discretion and convention
Recognition of party whips: Speaker decides which whip is valid in case of a split in a political party — critical for Tenth Schedule proceedings
UPSC trap: The 'merger' exception under the Tenth Schedule (merger of at least two-thirds of members) — Speaker decides whether a valid merger has occurred
Controversy: Speaker's partisan approach in recognizing splinter groups as the 'original party' to protect ruling coalition members from disqualification
